data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A genetic algorithm exploring mutations and recombinations of the known 45-comparator network, guided by partial sorting fitness (count of sorted 0-1 vectors out of 8192), can traverse the fitness landscape to discover a novel 44-comparator network for n=13 if one exists.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The fitness landscape of partial sorting networks is highly deceptive; counting sorted binary vectors does not provide a continuous gradient to the global optimum, causing the genetic algorithm to converge prematurely on 45-comparator local optima.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"Mutations that simply drop comparators strictly decrease sorting capability, and simultaneous compensatory structural mutations are statistically too rare to be discovered within a feasible genetic algorithm budget.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"Genetic algorithms inherently lack the systematic completeness of SAT-based or exhaustive search, meaning they cannot provide a discriminating experiment to prove the non-existence of 44-comparator networks.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Initialize a population of 45-comparator networks, potentially seeded by known optimal or near-optimal constructions. Evaluate fitness by running all 2^13 = 8192 binary vectors through each network and counting the number of correctly sorted outputs. Apply evolutionary operators: selection favoring networks with higher sorting success and fewer comparators, crossover combining sub-networks from different parents, and mutation perturbing individual comparator endpoints or deleting/inserting comparators. As the population evolves, the algorithm may identify and exploit structural symmetries (like reflection i -> n-1-i) and eliminate redundant comparators, yielding a structurally novel 44-comparator network.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
